items.body:
## Summary

Replaces the published +4 Ring of Tenacity benchmark with a **+3 Wand of Fireblast within the first 24 floors** — a query players actually run, and one that showcases the planner's strongest *exact* shortcut: only the Wandmaker can hand out a +3 wand, so Seed Seeker derives a depth-9 generation horizon and abandons seeds the moment the quest resolves without the wand, while the reference Java finder generates all 24 floors of every seed.

Depends on #22 (merged): the golden-mimic RNG parity fix is what makes the cross-check below exact.

## Changes

- `benchmark_query()` in the CLI now runs the wand query, so `cargo run --release -p shpd-seedfinder-cli -- --benchmark` reproduces the published chart.
- README headline (16–30×), chart caption/alt text, benchmarks table, and methodology rewritten for the new workload, including the strongest incumbent variant (manually depth-9-limited: 283 seeds/s, still 5.5× slower per core).
- `assets/benchmark.svg` updated in place (same design, palette validated for both color schemes; rendered and inspected in light and dark).

## Numbers (Apple M4 Pro, same day, same pinned v3.3.8 source for both finders)

| Configuration | Throughput | Relative |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Seed Seeker, 12 threads (1,000,000 seeds) | 13,716 seeds/s | **30.3×** |
| Seed Seeker, 1 thread (150,000 seeds) | 1,567 seeds/s | 16.7× per core |
| shpd-seed-finder, 6 processes (its best; 4→330, 8→373) | 453 seeds/s | 1× |

Add lockstep_vs_c.py: benchmark Lockstep against hand-written C
items.body:
## Summary

Adds a new native benchmark harness that compares Lockstep's shipped compiled code against idiomatic single-pass hand-written C implementations of the same workloads. This provides an honest external performance baseline rather than comparing Lockstep only against itself.

## Key Changes

- **New benchmark harness** (`benchmarks/native/lockstep_vs_c.py`):
  - Compiles real `.lock` workload sources to LLVM IR via `compile_lockstep`
  - Links against hand-written C reference kernels that compute the same transforms in single fused passes
  - Uses identical SoA arena layouts and byte offsets from generated headers
  - Primes two identical arenas with deterministic inputs and times both paths in the same process
  - Validates correctness by requiring output checksums to match before reporting results
  - Reports throughput (Mrows/s) and a portable `ratio = C time / Lockstep time` metric

- **Hand-written C references** for three workloads:
  - `particle_energy`: single fused kernel (baseline case)
  - `telemetry_filter_aggregation`: filter → shader+accumulate pipeline
  - `multi_stage_pipeline`: normalize → score → filter pipeline

- **Test coverage** (`tests/benchmarks/test_lockstep_vs_c.py`):
  - Smoke tests verifying the harness builds and runs with local clang
  - Cross-validates C reference checksums against the independent `run_native.py` harness
  - Skipped gracefully when clang is unavailable

- **Documentation and integration**:
  - Updated `benchmarks/RESULTS.md` with table 4 showing results (C wins every workload; ~20% on single kernel, ~5–6× on multi-stage pipelines)
  - Updated `benchmarks/native/README.md` with detailed explanation of the harness and what the gaps mean
  - Updated `benchmarks/README.md` to list the new harness alongside existing native benchmarks
  - Added `make bench-vs-c` target to Makefile
  - Added `lockstep-vs-c-results.json` to `.gitignore`

## Notable Implementation Details

- Reuses arena/offset parsing infrastructure from `run_native.py` to ensure consistency
- Generates a C driver that includes offset macros from the compiled header, allowing the reference to address columns by their generated names
- Portable timing: uses `clock_gettime` on POSIX systems and `QueryPerformanceCounter` on Windows
- Deterministic input priming matches `run_native.py` exactly for cross-validation
- Compiled with `clang -O3 -march=native -ffast-math` to match the reduction codegen and other native harnesses
- Results show the honest gap: Lockstep trails hand-written C due to byte-addressed pointer loads/stores vs. typed column walks, and multi-stage pipelines materialize intermediate streams instead of fusing through filters

items.title: ci(benchmark): Stop auto-updating the README comparison tables
items.body:
### What

Removes the three README auto-update steps from the benchmark workflow. The tables go back to being maintained by hand, which is what their methodology requires.

### Why

The README's benchmark tables are a **same-session** comparison — Abies and Blazor measured on the same machine in the same sitting. That's the only reason the Delta column means anything, and both the README and `blazor-baseline.json` say so:

> Measured with js-framework-benchmark **on the same machine, same session**.

> *"Static baseline — Blazor is not run in CI."*

CI structurally cannot produce a comparable figure. Blazor isn't run there, so the automated update could only swap the Abies column for shared-runner numbers while leaving Blazor's local numbers in place. On its first successful run it did exactly that:

| Benchmark | README (same-session) | CI-generated |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Create 1,000 rows | 119.5 ms (**+34%** vs Blazor) | 331.8 ms (**+291%**) |
| Create 10,000 rows | 1183.5 ms (**+47%**) | 3342.4 ms (**+336%**) |

Those deltas are the gap between a CI runner and a laptop, published as if the framework had regressed 4×. Merging that would have been worse than publishing nothing — it's a wrong number wearing the authority of automation.

It's the same error as the baseline problem in #341, one layer up: **comparability requires holding the measurement environment fixed.** #341 fixed it for CI-vs-CI; this fixes it for the README's local-vs-local.

### What still works

Nothing of value is lost. CI's valid contribution is Abies measured against its own history:

- the Abies-over-time trend still publishes to `gh-pages`
- the regression gate still compares CI against CI, with the smoothed baseline and 25% threshold from #341
- micro-benchmark throughput/allocation baselines still publish

Only the cross-framework table — which CI was never able to produce honestly — is no longer touched.

### Guardrails against re-adding it

- The reasoning is left **in the workflow** at the point where the steps used to be, with the actual numbers, so the next person sees why rather than re-adding it.
- `scripts/update-readme-benchmarks.py` stays as a local tool and its docstring now opens with **"RUN THIS LOCALLY, NOT IN CI"** plus the failure it causes.
- The README gains a short note that the tables are hand-maintained and why, pointing at the trends page for CI data.

### Follow-up for you

The stale `benchmark/readme-auto-update` branch still exists with that misleading diff on it. Worth deleting so nobody merges it later — say the word and I'll remove it, or delete it from the branches page.

### Testing

- `benchmark.yml` parses; the three README steps are gone (28 steps remain in `benchmark-check`, none matching README).
- No dangling references: nothing in `.github/` or `scripts/` invokes the removed steps.
- `update-readme-benchmarks.py` compiles and `--help` works — still usable locally.
- `DocSnippetCheck`: 31 compiled, 0 failed.

items.title: Implement Pure Python AVL Tree Backend, Update Benchmarks & Myths FAQ
items.body:
## Description
This PR resolves the behavioral inconsistency and benchmarking discrepancy between the C++ (Rust-compiled) backend and the pure Python fallback backend for sorted containers (`stl_set` and `stl_map`). 

### Problem
Previously, the Python implementations wrapped built-in `set` and `dict` objects. Because Python's built-ins are hash tables, they offered O(1) complexity and unordered iteration, whereas the Rust/C++ implementations used B-Trees with O(log n) complexity and sorted iteration. This resulted in behavioral inconsistencies (elements were sorted when Rust was compiled, but unsorted when it fell back to Python) and an unequal "apples-to-oranges" benchmark comparison.

### Solution
1. **AVL Tree Implementation:** Created a core self-balancing AVL Tree in pure Python to serve as the fallback backend for both set and map containers.
2. **Backend Unification:** Modified the private set and map implementation wrappers to use this AVL tree, ensuring O(log n) time complexity and sorted iteration on both Rust and Python backends.
3. **3-Way Benchmark:** Expanded the benchmark script to support a three-way comparison (Rust Backend vs. Pure Python Backend vs. Native Python Built-ins) to clearly document FFI boundary crossing costs and algorithmic tradeoffs.
4. **README FAQ:** Updated the README to address common myths regarding project utility (competitive programming compatibility) and the systems design benefits of the hybrid Rust-Python architecture.
5. **Version Bump:** Bumped versioning to 1.1.7 across configuration files.

## Changes
- **[NEW] pythonstl/core/avl_tree.py:** Self-balancing BST containing node insertion, balancing, deletions, and sorted in-order iterators.
- **[MODIFY] pythonstl/implementations/associative/_set_impl.py:** Replaced native set fallback with AVLTree.
- **[MODIFY] pythonstl/implementations/associative/_map_impl.py:** Replaced native dict fallback with AVLTree.
- **[MODIFY] benchmarks/benchmark_all_structures.py:** Added native built-in baseline and expanded the summary reporting table.
- **[MODIFY] README.md:** Added the 3-way container benchmark table and the Myths & Common Misconceptions FAQ.
- **[MODIFY] pythonstl/__init__.py & pyproject.toml:** Bumped version to 1.1.7.

## Verification
- Added test cases in tests/test_set.py and tests/test_map.py to verify that both backends maintain elements in sorted order.

items.title: Add SoA-vs-AoS layout micro-benchmark
items.body:
## Summary

This PR adds a micro-benchmark that quantifies the performance advantage of Lockstep's Struct-of-Arrays (SoA) memory layout over traditional Array-of-Structs (AoS). The benchmark runs identical branchless kernels over the same data in both layouts across a range of working-set sizes to isolate and measure the memory layout impact.

## Key Changes

- **New micro-benchmark script** (`benchmarks/native/soa_vs_aos.py`):
  - Generates and compiles C code that implements two kernels in both AoS and SoA layouts
  - `integrate` kernel: touches all fields (full physics step) — measures vectorization win
  - `energy` kernel: reads subset of fields (velocity + mass) — measures bandwidth win
  - Sweeps across configurable working-set sizes (default: 1K to 1M rows)
  - Verifies both layouts compute identical results before reporting timing ratios
  - Outputs throughput (Mrows/sec) and speedup ratios in table or JSON format
  - Compiled with `clang -O3 -march=native -ffast-math` to match Lockstep's codegen

- **Test suite** (`tests/benchmarks/test_soa_vs_aos.py`):
  - Smoke tests verifying the benchmark builds and runs with local clang
  - Validates that both layouts produce identical results
  - Confirms SoA is not slower than AoS for the fully-vectorizable kernel
  - Tests skipped gracefully when clang is unavailable

- **Documentation and build integration**:
  - Updated `benchmarks/native/README.md` with usage examples and explanation of the two kernels
  - Added `bench-soa` Makefile target for easy invocation
  - Updated `.gitignore` to exclude benchmark output JSON
  - Updated main `README.md` with reference to the new benchmark

## Implementation Details

- The benchmark uses a 6-float particle struct (24 bytes) matching the `particle_energy` workload
- Iteration counts scale inversely with problem size to ensure stable multi-millisecond samples across all sizes
- Results validation uses relative tolerance (1e-3) to account for floating-point rounding differences
- Supports custom compiler selection and output formats (table, JSON, or both)
- Designed to isolate memory layout as the only variable — kernels are branchless and data-independent

items.title: Add fusion probe benchmark to measure multi-stage pipeline overhead
items.body:
## Summary

This PR adds a micro-benchmark (`fusion_probe.py`) that quantifies the throughput penalty incurred by un-fused multi-stage pipelines. The benchmark compares two implementations of the same computation: one that mirrors current codegen behavior (separate loops per stage with materialized intermediates) and one that represents the optimizer's planned fused form (single loop with intermediates in registers).

## Key Changes

- **New benchmark tool** (`benchmarks/native/fusion_probe.py`): A Python-based micro-benchmark that:
  - Generates and compiles C code implementing both fused and unfused variants of a multi-stage pipeline
  - Runs both variants over identical SoA data and measures throughput (Mrows/sec)
  - Reports the speedup ratio between unfused and fused forms
  - Validates that both variants produce identical results before reporting metrics
  - Supports configurable row counts and iteration counts with automatic scaling

- **Test suite** (`tests/benchmarks/test_fusion_probe.py`): Smoke tests that:
  - Verify the probe builds and runs with the local clang compiler
  - Validate result agreement checking logic
  - Confirm fusion is not slower than the unfused baseline
  - Skip gracefully when clang is unavailable

- **Documentation and build integration**:
  - Updated `benchmarks/native/README.md` with detailed explanation of the fusion limitation and probe methodology
  - Added `bench-fusion` Makefile target for easy execution
  - Updated main `README.md` with reference to the new benchmark
  - Added `fusion-probe-results.json` to `.gitignore`

## Implementation Details

The benchmark addresses a specific codegen limitation: the `_can_vectorize_fused_group` check rejects any kernel with an `accum` parameter, causing pipelines like `multi_stage_pipeline` and `telemetry_filter_aggregation` to fall back to one strip-mined loop per stage instead of a single fused loop. This forces multiple passes over memory, materializing intermediate streams the optimizer planned to eliminate.

The C code template generates two implementations:
- **Unfused**: Three separate loops (Normalize → Score → KeepActive) that write and re-read intermediate arrays
- **Fused**: One loop that carries intermediates in registers and accumulates on the fly

Both are compiled with `-O3 -march=native -ffast-math` to match Lockstep's reduction codegen, ensuring the comparison isolates the effect of memory passes rather than other optimization differences.

Improve runtime trajectory result reporting and artifact schema
items.body:
### Motivation
- Make runtime trajectory run artifacts more structured and interpretable by replacing per-case JSONL streams with JSON array artifacts and richer run-level metrics. 
- Surface runtime-trajectory metrics (safety, controller, reliability, auditability) alongside harness pass/fail so runs are mechanically useful and human-readable. 
- Document artifact semantics and claim boundaries so simulated controller outcomes and unsupported metrics are clearly disclosed.

### Description
- Update `benchmarks/core/runtime_trajectories/runner.py` to accumulate per-case records in memory and write `raw_responses.json`, `normalized_results.json`, and `trajectory_results.json` as JSON arrays, and to stop writing `.jsonl` per-case streams. 
- Add scoring and reporting helpers in the runner: `_rate`, `build_scores`, and `build_summary`, which compute the expanded `scores.json` structure (case mix, `harness`, `signal_detection`, `decision_compatibility`, `controller_outcome`, `operational_reliability`, `auditability`, and `not_measured`) and render a structured human-readable `summary.md`. 
- Preserve `manifest.json`, `scores.json`, and `summary.md` (now with richer content), and ensure `trajectory_results.json` is explicitly documented as a simulated benchmark trajectory artifact and not a production audit log. 
- Keep existing client header fix by setting default headers in `benchmarks/lib/api_client.py` (`User-Agent: inhibitor-lab-benchmark/0.1`, `Accept: application/json`). 
- Update `benchmarks/core/runtime_trajectories/cases.jsonl` to include `block` as an acceptable decision for the excessive-agency fixture and expect `controller_action: block_original` and `original_action_executed: false`. 
- Update docs to reflect the new artifact names and semantics in `benchmarks/core/runtime_trajectories/README.md`, `benchmarks/README.md`, and reporting docs under `benchmarks/reporting/` so they state that per-case runtime-trajectory artifacts are JSON arrays, `summary.md` is the human-readable run report, controller/mock-tool outcomes are simulated, and unsupported metrics appear under `not_measured` in `scores.json`.

### Testing
- Ran `python3 benchmarks/validate_fixtures.py` and it passed for the repository fixtures. ✅
- Ran `python3 benchmarks/run_all.py --suite runtime_trajectories --dry-run` to verify dry-run behavior and case loading, which reported the planned cases successfully. ✅
- Compiled relevant modules with `python3 -m py_compile benchmarks/lib/api_client.py benchmarks/core/runtime_trajectories/*.py` to ensure syntax correctness and the new client headers, which succeeded. ✅
- Performed a local non-networked check constructing fake result records and ran `build_scores` / `build_summary` to verify JSON-serializable output and expected numeric computations (latency mean, prevention rate); assertions passed. ✅
- Ran `git diff --check` to ensure no whitespace or diff issues; remaining checks passed. ✅
